screens.heading: Data lives in many tables
screens.body:
Good databases split data across tables — Students here, Enrollments there. That's clean design, but questions span tables: 'which courses is Ava taking?'

JOINs answer cross-table questions by matching rows through their keys. They're the reason foreign keys exist: the keys are the meeting points.
screens.keyPoint: JOINs reunite data that normalization split apart.

check.question: You JOIN tables to…
options: Answer questions that span multiple tables

screens.heading: Foreign keys make JOINs possible
screens.body:
A JOIN matches rows where a foreign key equals a primary key: Enrollments.student_id = Students.student_id. The keys are the bridge.

Without that link, the database can't know which enrollment belongs to which student. Design the keys right, and JOINs become natural.
screens.keyPoint: JOINs walk across the foreign-key bridges.

check.question: Enrollments JOIN Students ON Enrollments.student_id = Students.student_id matches rows where…

screens.heading: INNER JOIN: matches only
screens.body:
INNER JOIN returns only rows with a match on both sides. Students INNER JOIN Enrollments shows students who enrolled — students with no enrollments vanish.

It's the default JOIN and the most common. If you just write JOIN, you get an INNER JOIN.
screens.keyPoint: INNER JOIN keeps only matched rows.

code.snippet:
SELECT Students.name, Courses.title
FROM Students
JOIN Enrollments
  ON Students.student_id = Enrollments.student_id
JOIN Courses
  ON Enrollments.course_code = Courses.course_code;

screens.heading: LEFT JOIN: keep every left row
screens.body:
LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left (first) table, even with no match — unmatched spots fill with NULL. 'All students, with their enrollments if any.'

This is how you find what's missing: add WHERE Enrollments.student_id IS NULL and you get students who enrolled in nothing.
screens.keyPoint: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows; gaps become NULL.

code.snippet:
SELECT Students.name, Enrollments.course_code
FROM Students
LEFT JOIN Enrollments
  ON Students.student_id = Enrollments.student_id;

check.question: A LEFT JOIN from Students to Enrollments shows…
options: Every student, with NULLs where there's no enrollment

screens.heading: RIGHT, FULL, and self JOINs
screens.body:
RIGHT JOIN is LEFT JOIN mirrored — it keeps all rows from the right table. FULL JOIN keeps everything from both sides, with NULLs wherever there's no match.

A self-JOIN joins a table to itself: Employees JOIN Employees pairs each person with their manager, using the manager_id foreign key. Same table, two roles.
screens.keyPoint: RIGHT mirrors LEFT; FULL keeps both; self-JOIN pairs rows in one table.

screens.heading: Constraints guard relationships
screens.body:
Constraints are rules the database enforces. NOT NULL bans empties, UNIQUE bans duplicates, CHECK enforces conditions.

Foreign-key constraints are special: they forbid orphan rows. You can't insert an enrollment for student 999 if no student 999 exists — the database rejects it.
screens.keyPoint: Constraints reject bad data before it lands.

code.snippet: student_id INT NOT NULL REFERENCES Students(student_id)

screens.heading: JOIN pitfalls
screens.body:
Two classic mistakes: forgetting the ON clause gives a cross join — every row matched to every row, exploding your results. And joining on the wrong column silently returns wrong answers.

Also watch duplicates: if the 'many' side has three rows, the 'one' side's data repeats three times. That's normal — but don't COUNT(*) it without thinking.

check.question: Forgetting the ON clause in a JOIN produces…
options: A cross join — every row paired with every row
